Noah M.
Daniels I ask you to consider my candidacy for the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for a 2-year term, 2026-2028.
I am an associate professor of computer science, and will have been a member of the faculty for 10 years as of Fall 2026.
I am beginning my second term on the Faculty Senate, and just completing my first 1-year term on FSEC.
In my first term on Faculty Senate, I served two years as chair of the Committee on Technology and Infrastructure.
In that time, my primary focus was on developing consensus policies for ITS to replace unilaterally-developed policies set forth by the administration which hindered academic freedom, research, and teaching.
I have continued this effort as the FSEC liaison to CTI.
This has culminated in a draft of the new ITS policy (with several flaws noted by the faculty) presented for comment in the last month.

In my time on CTI and FSEC, I have served on the IT Governance committee, on the search committees for the Chief Information Officer as well as the University Librarian, and am a founding member of the ad-hoc committees to proactively evaluate whether the technologies on which we depend are effective before the administration signs lengthy contracts.
I enjoy bringing my own perspective to these intellectually diverse working groups, and reconciling that perspective with those of others.
I see the particular strengths I bring to FSEC as including a deep understanding of both technology and how people use technology, as well as a bulwark to efforts to corporatize university ITS and other aspects of university life.
In a tumultuous time when new cybersecurity threats lead to sometimes-draconian policies that can impact research and teaching, as well as the rise of “AI” everywhere (sometimes without the needed critical thinking), I believe I can bring expertise and reasoned argument to addressing these issues.
Beyond technology, I see the adoption of the new budget model and the recent, eye-opening budget committee survey as being a key concern of FSEC going forward.
I believe we must work with the administration to address specific concerns brought to light by that survey, outreach to faculty, and other data such as the explosion of new course proposals. 1

Off-campus conduct shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the Student Discipline System if one of the following conditions is met: 1) an infraction of a community standard of behavior as listed in the STUDENT HANDBOOK occurs at: a) an ofﬁcial University event, such as a ﬁeld trip; b) a University sanctioned event as deﬁned in Section 8.51.12 of the UNIVERSITY MANUAL; or c) an event sponsored by a recognized student organization, fraternity or sorority; or 2) an off-campus action performed by a person while he or she is a student is of a nature such that it would be subject to the Student Discipline System if it had occurred on campus, and the nature and circumstances of the infraction provide reasonable grounds for believing that the alleged offender posed or poses a threat to life, health, or safety of the University community, or to University property the safety of self or others or if the alleged offender is repeatedly arrested or cited for violating local, state or federal laws.

The decision to apply jurisdiction to off-campus conduct shall be made by the Dean of Students.
Rationale: Broadens University’ s ability to act to protect safety of students and others. 17 out of 17 state colleges and universities regarded as peer institutions have jurisdiction policies that are broader than that recommended above.
The proposed policy gives the University slightly broader discretion to decide whether or not to apply jurisdiction.
As indicated in the policy revision, safety will be a signiﬁcant consideration.
In addition, the Manual already provides a process with which to appeal the application of jurisdiction.

Administrative Report January 2017, Administrative Report February 2021 1.20.11 Composition of the Board Trustees and Quorum Requirements.
The Board of Trustees shall consist of seventeen (17) voting members and four (4) non-voting ex officio members, including one (1) URI faculty member and one (1) URI student to be appointed by the President, and the chair of the Rhode Island Board of Education and the chair of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education.
The members shall be appointed in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2, which specifies that the governor will appoint the members with the advice and consent of the senate, and with due consideration to recommendations from the President of the University.

At least three (3) of the members appointed by the governor shall be residents of the state of Rhode Island, at least one (1) of those members shall be selected from a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives, and at least one (1) of those members shall be selected from a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the president of the senate.
The President of the University of Rhode Island will appoint one (1) faculty member and one (1) student member who shall be a full-time student in good standing at the University, and who shall both serve in non-voting, ex officio capacity for a single two (2) year term.
Six (6) of the members initially appointed pursuant to RIGL Section 16-32-2.2 shall serve terms of three (3) years; seven (7) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of two (2) years, including the member appointed from the list submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives and the member appointed from the list submitted by the president of the senate; and four (4) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of one (1) year.

After the initial terms of appointment have expired, the governor shall appoint nine (9) members with the advice and consent of the senate to serve as members of the board with two (2) members appointed for a term of three (3) years; with two (2) members appointed for a term of two (2) years, including the member appointed from the list submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives and the member appointed from the list submitted by the president of the senate; and with two (2) members appointed for a term of one (1) year and shall be eligible to be reappointed for a

term of two (2) years.
The remaining eight (8) voting members shall be self-perpetuating members appointed by the Board pursuant to rules adopted by the Board regarding the nomination and appointment of members and shall serve terms as defined by the Board pursuant to the adopted rules and shall be eligible for reappointment.
In making the appointments of self-perpetuating members, the Board shall give due consideration to recommendations from the President of the University.
A quorum shall consist of thirteen (13) voting members of the Board, but less than a quorum may adjourn any meetings.
A majority vote of those present and voting shall be required for action.
A majority of the members of the Board shall elect the chair of the Board in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2(c) from among the voting members of the Board.
In addition, the members of the Board shall elect a vice chair.
The terms of office shall be three years or until a duly appointed successor is elected.
Administrative Report January 2017, Administrative Report February 2021 1.20.12 Chief Responsibilities of the Board of Trustees.

The Board of Trustees (“Board”) is established by act of the Rhode Island General Assembly as the exclusive fiduciary authority for the University of Rhode Island (“University” or “URI”).
In that capacity, the Board is legally entrusted with the institution’s care and has the critical responsibility for protecting the integrity of the institution’s mission as Rhode Island’s premier institution of higher education and overseeing compliance with all provisions of the law.

To meet its statutory mandate as the ultimate governing authority for the University of Rhode Island, the Board of Trustees performs a number of critical functions, including but not limited to: ● Appointment of trustees, consistent with the standards and limitations set forth in the enabling statute; ● Appointment and evaluation of the President of the University; ● Review and approval of the Academic Strategic Plan and the three-year funding plan for the University, which is to be developed and submitted to the Board by the President; ● Upon receipt of the recommendations of the President and appropriate faculty bodies, approval of the awarding of degrees (including honorary degrees, diplomas, certificates and honors to be conferred by the President); ● Approval of recommendations made by the President regarding the awarding of tenure and promotion to qualified members of the University faculty; ● Review of the University’s performance under the institution’s Academic Strategic Plan developed and reported by the President and university community;

● Stewardship of University physical, financial, and human resources consistent with the provisions of all applicable statutes and regulations and policies of the Board of Trustees; ● Promoting and enforcing integrity and effectiveness of all aspects of the University’s budgeting and financial management, including changes in tuition and fees, submission and approval of the University’s annual budget and three-year financial projections; ● Approve the creation or termination of new academic majors and the creation, consolidation or termination of academic departments, schools and colleges based on the recommendations of the President who shall have followed the appropriate University process.
Administrative Report January 2017, Administrative Report February 2021 The President of the University 1.30.10 Presidential Powers—Shared Governance.
In 2014, the President of the University received authority over certain items that previously needed to be submitted for approval to the super-ordinated state body (Board of Governors, Board of Regents, etc.).

The items over which the President now has authority include: “To create, and consolidate departments, divisions, programs, and courses of study within the university with the assistance of the commissioner of postsecondary education within the approved role and scope adopted by the council on postsecondary education pursuant to § 16-59-4” This authority was reaffirmed in 2019 upon passage of legislation forming the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees (see RI General Law § 16-32-2.1).
The law stipulates, however, that this authority is to be exercised “consistent with shared governance practices, [and] in conformity with § 16-32-10,” which states that it “shall also be the duty of the president and a committee of the faculty, . . . to arrange courses of study conforming to all acts of Congress, and prescribe any qualifications for the admission of students and any rules of study, exercise, discipline, and government as the president and committee may deem proper.” Since 1960, the committee of the faculty mentioned in this legislation has been understood to be the URI Faculty Senate.

We honor and respect the enduring and continuing relationship between the Indigenous peoples and this land by teaching and learning more about their history and present-day communities, and by becoming stewards of the land we, now too, inhabit.” #22-23-2 1.10.20 Background.
The University of Rhode Island, the state’s land and sea grant research institution began as the state of Rhode Island’s Agricultural Experiment Station and agricultural school chartered in 1888.

In 1892, the institution’s name was changed to the Rhode Island College of Agriculture and the Mechanic Arts.
This name was subsequently changed to Rhode Island State College in 1909.
The current name- the University of Rhode Island— was adopted in 1951 by an act of the State of Rhode Island’s General Assembly.
For a complete history of the University, refer to https://www.uri.edu/about/history/. 1.10.30 Mission.
The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives.
A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and to develop informed residents and leaders.
URI is committed to high-quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges.
Situated on the traditional land and territories of

the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members. 1.10.40 Values.
The University of Rhode Island is committed to the following foundational values: ● Freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good. ● An inclusive, accessible, equitable and diverse community whereby we respect the rights anddignity of all. ● Intellectual curiosity, lifelong learning, leadership, and scholarship in creating a thriving URI community in service to Rhode Island and the world. ● Sustainability and care of our environment conducive to the physical and mental health of our community. ● Self- and institutional reflection of our values in our work, scholarship and interactions, holding ourselves, each other, and the institution accountable to uphold them to a high standard.

UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEE Report #2005-06-2 February 3, 2006 At the direction of the Faculty Senate, the Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee (CBUM) drafted Manual language to account for a procedure for new programs that have no additional resources attached to them.
This issue originally came to the Faculty Senate from the Graduate Council.
The CBUM Committee drafted changes to University Manual section 8.85.30 and the addition of a new 8.85.31.
These were forwarded to the Curricular Affairs Committee and Graduate Council for their consideration.
The Graduate Council approved the changes on November 18, 2005 and the Curricular Affairs Committee approved them on November 21, 2005.
Following notification by the CAC and the Graduate Council that the Manual changes are satisfactory to both committees, the Constitution, By Laws and University Manual Committee is ready to recommend their approval to the Faculty Senate at this time.

The CBUM Committee recommends that the Faculty Senate approve the following changes to the UNIVERSITY MANUAL on classification of new programs: A.Rename section 8.85.30 Classification of Programs: 8.85.30 Classification of Programs for which new funding is required … B.
Add new section 8.85.31 8.85.31 Programs for which no new funding is required.
When the proponents of a new program, including a certificate program, assert that the new venture can be administered entirely with existing funds, the proposal shall include a five- year plan demonstrating that existing funds are sufficient for carrying the program.
Prior to that plan being presented to the Faculty Senate Curricular Affairs Committee or the Graduate Council, it shall be reviewed and approved by the appropriate department(s) and college(s) whose participation is necessary for the program to be offered successfully.
The plan shall also include a Budget Office review.
No classification under 8.85.30 is required.

UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND AD HOC COMMITTEE ON SECTIONS 8.87.10-11 OF THE UNIVERSITY MANUAL On February 22, 2007, the Faculty Senate established an ad hoc committee in response to President Carothers’ veto of Senate Bill #06- 07--10 “Abolition of Programs Legislation on Suspension of Academic Programs.” The charge to the committee was to review 8.87.10 and 8.87.11 of the UNIVERSITY MANUAL with the intention of crafting new legislation that would satisfy both the Administration and the Faculty Senate.
The five member ad hoc committee was comprised of three members of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee, James Kinnie, James Miller and Michael Rice; a designee of the President, Dean Winifred Brownell; and a designee of the Provost, Vice Provost Lynn Pasquerella.
The ad hoc committee met in early April 2007 and decided to revise the proposed section 8.87.12 Suspension of Programs.
Once a revised section 8.87.12 was agreed upon, the committee decided that sections 8.87.10-11 no longer needed revision.
The ad hoc committee recommends that the Faculty Senate approve the following proposed new section 8.87.12 Suspension of Programs: 8.87.12 Suspension of Programs.

The President has the prerogative of suspending admissions of students into degree granting programs.
The President shall notify the University Community, including Admissions Officers, and the Board of Governors for Higher Education as to the reasons for and the effective date of program suspension, taking into account students already admitted for study.
In concert with policies of the Board of Governors for Higher Education, programs may be maintained in a state of suspension for a maximum of 6 years.
Programs may be removed from suspension by the President at any time prior to the expiration of the time limit.
The President may appeal to the Board of Governors for Higher Education for a three (3) year extension beyond the prescribed time limit.
After the time limit for program suspension has been reached, procedures for program abolition set forth in Section 8.87.10 shall be followed.

PROGRAM REPORT CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE Report 2025-2026-08B At the April 23, 2026 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES BA – Computer Science, effective Fall 2026 Appendix A This curriculum revision represents a strategic modernization that strengthens the B.A. in Computer Science through internal reallocation of Department resources while preserving its distinctive character as a flexible, interdisciplinary degree option.
The proposed changes maintain 120 total credits while prescribing a 36-credit core.
The B.A. requires nine core CS courses compared to eleven core and three specialization courses in the B.S. program, providing a lighter computing load while ensuring foundational competency in software development, algorithms, systems, and machine learning.
BA – Film Media, effective Summer 2026 Appendix B Film media is deleting courses that have been removed from the URI catalog and adding new FLM courses to the appropriate elective pools.

BA – Journalism, effective Fall 2026 Appendix C During a curriculum retreat, members of the journalism faculty evaluated both the program learning outcomes and the curriculum for the B.A in Journalism degree program.
Based on our retreat and our focus on experiential learning in the program, we voted to adopt new requirements for our major.
These changes include eliminating the conceptual/skills designation in our current curriculum, adding additional core requirements, and altering JOR elective options so that students may pursue recommended, but not required, pathways in print, photojournalism, and multimedia/video journalism.
Several advanced courses will work directly with our new Community News Lab, which provides real-world experience to our students by having them produce news content for local media organizations.

BA – Public Relations, effective Fall 2026 Appendix D The Public Relations degree program was developed within the Communication Studies department.
In the Fall of 2024, the program moved into a new department.
The Department of Journalism and Public Relations now manages both the Journalism BA and Public Relations BA degrees.
While the PR program stands on its own, it shares many courses with Communication Studies, particularly in the three focus areas.
As the two programs have become more distinct, scheduling and course management issues have arisen.
Public Relations majors have trouble enrolling in Communication Studies courses to fulfill their focus areas.
We are proposing to amend the focus areas so s tudents have more flexibility in their elective courses.
Both the JOR/PR faculty and the Communication Studies faculty support the proposed changes (please see attached).
Please note the focus area course list remains the same with one exception, we added an additional course COM 321G.
BA – Theatre, effective Fall 2026 Appendix E The Theatre BA is currently suspended and only open to those students who are pursuing a degree in Elementary Education.

We propose reinstating the BA for all eligible students in order to serve the shifting demographic of our student body as well as refine our BFA program to introduce more rigorous standards appropriate to a pre-professional training program.
The Rhode Island Promise Act has increased the number of transfer students considerably, making it highly difficult for those students to complete a BFA in 4 years.
Additionally, the number of double majors/minors has increased making it equally difficult for those students to complete the very narrow BFA curriculum without impact to their other majors (particularly those, such as Nursing, who also have to meet clinical requirements that tend to conflict with our required courses).
A BA offers more flexibility for order of courses, thus making it more feasible for our transfer students and those completing more than one major.
URI Theatre completed an External Review in Spring of 2024.
Among their recommendations was to standardize evaluation tools across our curriculum and instate more rigorous standards for degree completion, including capstone performances and projects.

Many BFA programs also involve standards that, if not met, result in dismissal from the program.
It has never been the policy of URI theatre to dismiss students from our program except in very rare cases of academic failure.
Introducing this type of standardization is possible if we have the option to invite students to our BA program in the event that the BFA curriculum is not a good fit.
Bifurcating our program in this way allows URI Theatre to serve the widest number of students while also introducing more clear standards for our BFA students.
The reinstatement of the BA does not require any new courses or staffing.
Students in the BA program will be taking courses already offered in our existing curriculum but have more choice in terms of when and what they take.

Because our program has undergone some changes to course codes since the suspension of the BA, we include here the courses we propose for completion of the BA in Theatre: Core Courses (total of 33 credits): THE111 (Introduction to Acting), THE161 (Introduction to Stagecraft), THE181 (Script Analysis), THE221 (Introduction to Stage Management), THE250 (Costume Laboratory), THE251 (Introduction to Design), THE307 or THE338G ( Creative Dramatics or Ethics in Theatre), THE321 (Orientation to Directing), THE381 (Theatre History to 1642), THE382 (Theatre History:

Neoclassical through 19th century), and either THE351, 352, 383, 384 OR 481 (these are advanced design or special topics courses) for a total of 33 required credits.
Optional electives within the major include THE112, THE200, THE300, THE400.
For many students, this would include participating in our production season for which they receive course credit (THE200/300/400).
Students must complete a minimum of 30 credits at the 300-level or above (these may include 300-level courses offered inside the major or courses offered outside the program).
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES BS – Clinical Neuroscience, effective Fall 2026 Appendix F INP Curriculum Committee voted unanimously in favor of having this course, BPS/PSY 436: Psychotropic Drugs and Therapy as a track elective for clinical neuroscience students.
This course would benefit our clinical neuroscience students from knowledge regarding psychotropics medications that are used to treat clinical disorders (depression, anxiety, OCD, etc.) Many of the clinical neuroscience students pursue healthcare, graduate PhD programs in psychology, and medical school.
Support letter from PSY is attached.

Editorial update to remove duplicate admission requirement information from the main program description.
Updated UCAS to FISS.
BS – Dietetics, effective Fall 2026 Appendix G The Nutrition department has put forth a new course, NUT 396, to streamline what was formerly covered in two courses (NUT 394 and 395).
This course is currently awaiting final Faculty Senate approval with first offering in Spring 2027.
To align with this, the curriculum beginning with the 2026/2027 catalog year will be updated to reflect this change.
BS – Nutrition, effective Fall 2026 Appendix H When making updates to the BS Nutrition and specializations, NUT 444 was inadvertently left off the list of required core courses.
It has now been added to the required core Nutrition courses, totaling 34 NUT core credits.
Adding NUT 444 was approved in bill CASC 25-26-04B.
This update is to modify core Nutrition course requirements for both Nutrition Science and Pre-Health tracks.
The department has proposed combining NUT 394 Lifecycle Nutrition I and NUT 395 Lifecycle Nutrition II into a one-semester course, NUT 396 Nutrition in the Lifecycle.
This reduces the total required core NUT credits to 31 and increases free elective credits by 3.

COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING BS – Civil Engineering, effective Fall 2026 Appendix I Changes: (1) there was a change in the number and credit count of a required course; changed EGR 105 (1 cr) to EGR 101 (2 cr) and updated the total number of program credits. This is a college-wide change. (2) updated the admission requirements to the major by eliminating EGR 105/106. This is a college-wide change. (3) added footnote related to EGR 101 (4) Replace STA 409 with ISE 311 (Prob. & Statistics for Engineers) since it is designed for engineers (5) Add EGR 316G (Engineering Ethics) instead of two General Education Outcomes - Ethics is a topic on the FE Exam (6) Remove CVE 400 (ethics component replaced by EGR 316G) (7) Add CVE 460 Steel Structures - required topic on the FE Exam (8) Add CVE 484 as option for professional elective COLLEGE OF PHARMACY BS – Medicinal Neuroscience, effective Fall 2026 Appendix J The objective of implementing these changes was to ensure students had courses within COP that they could take for their major/elective credits that were offered annually. This was a major complaint of Medicinal Neuroscience students previously, and in order to increase the number of students in the track we want to provide a curriculum that is robust but also offered each year. The INP curriculum committee voted on these changes in February 2026.

Kingston Proposed Summer 2026 Existing Fall 2025 Changes Program Description The Major.
Film/Media is an interdisciplinary major offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory.
Our curriculum reflects the dynamic and diverse nature of this field, approached from a perspective of film history and media theory.
Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including film, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts.
A wide range of courses is available to the film/media student—courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.

The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies, either in film and media production for an M.F.A., or in a master’s or doctoral program in film and media studies.
Students majoring in film/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
All students must complete the core courses: FLM 110, FLM 203 (or ENG 302), FLM 204 (or FLM 205 or 206), including the senior-level seminar FLM 495 (or FLM 496); a minimum of 6 credits from the production and technique category and 6 credits from the critical studies category; a minimum of 3 elective credits in courses that count toward the film major from the Production and Technique and Critical Studies categories (see below).
This wide range of choices in film/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.

Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the film media program before beginning their coursework in the major.
